content: Peripheral intravenous cannulation is a fundamental and frequently performed medical procedure. However, achieving successful cannulation can sometimes be challenging when using the traditional landmark method. Ultrasound guidance, which is already a standard for central venous cannulation, has been proposed as an alternative for peripheral venous cannulation, but its effectiveness and safety in this context remain uncertain. The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness and safety of ultrasound guidance versus the landmark method for peripheral intravenous cannulation in adults. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that directly compared these two methods. The primary outcomes assessed were first-pass success of cannulation, overall success of cannulation, and pain. Secondary outcomes included procedure time for first-pass and overall cannulation, the number of attempts required, patient satisfaction, and overall complications. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The study included 14 RCTs and 2 quasi-RCTs, involving a total of 2,267 participants. Participants were categorized based on the difficulty of cannulation using the landmark method: difficult, moderate, or easy. The majority of studies focused on difficult participants, with fewer studies addressing moderate or easy cases. The risk of bias across studies ranged from low to high, with concerns primarily related to blinding for subjective outcomes. For participants classified as difficult, ultrasound guidance significantly increased the likelihood of first-pass success (risk ratio [RR] 1.50, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.15 to 1.95) and overall success of cannulation (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.77). However, there was no clear difference in reported pain levels (mean difference [MD] -0.20, 95% CI -1.13 to 0.72). Ultrasound guidance was associated with a longer procedure time for first-pass cannulation (MD 119.9 seconds, 95% CI 88.6 to 151.1) and improved patient satisfaction (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.49, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.92). It also reduced the number of cannulation attempts (MD -0.33, 95% CI -0.64 to -0.02). There was no significant difference in the procedure time for overall cannulation (MD -24.9 seconds, 95% CI -323.1 to 273.3) or in overall complications (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.10). For participants classified as moderate, ultrasound guidance increased first-pass success (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.27). There was no significant difference in pain levels (MD 0.10, 95% CI -0.47 to 0.67). The procedure time for first-pass cannulation was longer with ultrasound guidance (MD 95.2 seconds, 95% CI 72.8 to 117.6). No studies assessed overall success of cannulation, the number of attempts, patient satisfaction, or the procedure time for overall cannulation in this subgroup. There was no significant difference in overall complications (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.82). For participants classified as easy, ultrasound guidance was associated with a decrease in first-pass success (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.85 to 0.94). Pain levels were higher with ultrasound guidance (MD 0.60, 95% CI 0.17 to 1.03). The procedure time for first-pass cannulation was longer (MD 94.8 seconds, 95% CI 81.2 to 108.5). No studies assessed overall success of cannulation, the number of attempts, patient satisfaction, or the procedure time for overall cannulation in this subgroup. There was no significant difference in overall complications (RR 2.48, 95% CI 0.90 to 6.87). In conclusion, the evidence suggests that ultrasound guidance may provide benefits for difficult participants by increasing first-pass and overall success rates, with no significant difference in pain levels. For moderate participants, ultrasound guidance may offer a small improvement in first-pass success, again with no significant difference in pain. However, for easy participants, ultrasound guidance appears to decrease first-pass success and increase pain, with no clear benefit in other outcomes. The certainty of the evidence varies across outcomes and participant subgroups, ranging from very low to high.
